# Assemblies {#sec-assemblies}

::: {.chapter-abstract}
A bracket and two pins, exported as one file of 335 records.
Where the tree is, where the positions are, why they are kept apart, and the second way exporters do it.
:::

The clamp is the bracket of @sec-curves-surfaces-hole-in-bracket with two pins standing on it: one at x = 15, one at x = 45, both on the top face (@fig-clamp).
As a STEP file it has three products but only two solids' worth of geometry — the pin's geometry appears once, not twice — and about forty records of structure that say how they fit together.
This chapter is about those forty.

![`clamp.step`, drawn by placing each component where the file's transformations put it: the bracket once, the pin twice.](../figures/clamp.svg){#fig-clamp width=60%}

## Three product chains {#sec-assemblies-product-chains}

The file opens the way every file does, with a product chain.
Then it has two more:

```{.step source="clamp.step"}
#5 = PRODUCT_DEFINITION('design','',#6,#9);
#7 = PRODUCT('CLAMP-ASSY','CLAMP-ASSY','',(#8));
    ...
#35 = PRODUCT_DEFINITION('design','',#36,#39);
#37 = PRODUCT('bracket','bracket','',(#38));
    ...
#243 = PRODUCT_DEFINITION('design','',#244,#247);
#245 = PRODUCT('pin-1','pin-1','',(#246));
```

Each has its own formation, its own pair of contexts, its own category record.
`#5` is the assembly's definition, `#35` the bracket's, `#243` the pin's.
Nothing in these records relates them to one another.
The pin's product is called `'pin-1'` rather than `'pin'` — the exporter took the name of the first instance it met as the name of the part — which is the kind of thing you learn to expect from assembly exports and which the structure below does not depend on.

Each product also has its shape.
The bracket's and pin's are `ADVANCED_BREP_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION`s containing solids, exactly as in the single-part files.
The assembly's is different:

```{.step source="clamp.step"}
#3 = SHAPE_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION(#4,#10);
#4 = PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE('','',#5);
#10 = SHAPE_REPRESENTATION('',(#11,#15,#19,#23),#27);
#11 = AXIS2_PLACEMENT_3D('',#12,#13,#14);        /* origin */
#15 = AXIS2_PLACEMENT_3D('',#16,#17,#18);        /* (0,0,0): the bracket goes here */
#19 = AXIS2_PLACEMENT_3D('',#20,#21,#22);        /* (15,10,10): pin-1 goes here */
#23 = AXIS2_PLACEMENT_3D('',#24,#25,#26);        /* (45,10,10): pin-2 goes here */
```

The assembly has no solid.
Its shape representation is a plain `SHAPE_REPRESENTATION` whose items are four coordinate frames: its own origin and one target position for each child.
The geometry of an assembly *is* the geometry of its children, placed.
This representation is the assembly's coordinate space, and the placements in it are the only numbers in the whole structure.

## The tree: `NEXT_ASSEMBLY_USAGE_OCCURRENCE` {#sec-assemblies-tree}

The parent–child relationships are three records:

```{.step source="clamp.step"}
#239 = NEXT_ASSEMBLY_USAGE_OCCURRENCE('1','bracket','',#5,#35,$);
#311 = NEXT_ASSEMBLY_USAGE_OCCURRENCE('2','pin-1','',#5,#243,$);
#317 = NEXT_ASSEMBLY_USAGE_OCCURRENCE('3','pin-2','',#5,#243,$);
```

The schema, through three levels of inheritance:

```express
ENTITY product_definition_relationship;
  id                          : identifier;
  name                        : label;
  description                 : OPTIONAL text;
  relating_product_definition : product_definition;     -- the parent
  related_product_definition  : product_definition;     -- the child
END_ENTITY;

ENTITY product_definition_usage
  SUBTYPE OF (product_definition_relationship);
END_ENTITY;

ENTITY assembly_component_usage
  SUBTYPE OF (product_definition_usage);
  reference_designator : OPTIONAL identifier;
END_ENTITY;

ENTITY next_assembly_usage_occurrence
  SUBTYPE OF (assembly_component_usage);
END_ENTITY;
```

`NEXT_ASSEMBLY_USAGE_OCCURRENCE` declares nothing of its own; all six parameters are inherited.
Six parameters: an id, a name, a description, the **relating** (parent) definition, the **related** (child) definition, and an optional reference designator.
One record is one **occurrence** of one child inside one parent.
These records form a directed acyclic graph of product definitions, with a separate edge for each usage.
The occurrence tree is that graph expanded from a root; a reused subassembly is expanded once per occurrence, each with its own world transform.
There is no record for "the assembly structure" as a whole; there are only edges, and the tree is whatever they add up to.

Three things to notice.

`#311` and `#317` both have `#243` as their child.
The pin is **defined once and used twice**.
This is the distinction a bill of materials rests on: one product definition, two occurrences.
The BOM line for the pin has quantity 2 because two NAUOs point at it, and there is one pin geometry in the file, not two.

The `name` attribute carries the **instance name** — `'pin-1'`, `'pin-2'` — which is how the CAD system distinguished the two occurrences in its tree.
The part's own name is on the `PRODUCT` record.
In this file they collide (`'pin-1'` is both the product name and the first instance name) because of the exporter's naming choice; in a SolidWorks or NX export the product would be `'PIN'` and the instances `'PIN-1'` and `'PIN-2'`.

The `reference_designator` is `$`.
It is meant for the position label on an electrical schematic or a drawing balloon — `'R12'`, `'B3'` — and most mechanical exporters leave it empty.

A tree with only NAUOs is unplaced.
The NAUOs say nothing about where each child sits; a viewer that draws them at the parent's origin is falling back, not reading a placement.
Position is a separate structure, attached to each NAUO from the side.

## The position: five records per occurrence {#sec-assemblies-position}

For the bracket:

```{.step source="clamp.step"}
#238 = PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE('Placement','Placement of an item',#239);
#235 = CONTEXT_DEPENDENT_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION(#236,#238);
#236 = ( REPRESENTATION_RELATIONSHIP('','',#40,#10)
         REPRESENTATION_RELATIONSHIP_WITH_TRANSFORMATION(#237)
         SHAPE_REPRESENTATION_RELATIONSHIP() );
#237 = ITEM_DEFINED_TRANSFORMATION('','',#11,#15);
#15 = AXIS2_PLACEMENT_3D('',#16,#17,#18);        /* in the assembly's representation */
```

Reading it from the NAUO outward:

**`#238`** is a `PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE` whose `definition` is the NAUO `#239` rather than a product definition.
@sec-product-to-shape said the `definition` attribute is a SELECT that admits either; this is the other case.
It means: *the occurrence of the bracket in the clamp has a shape*.
The strings `'Placement'` and `'Placement of an item'` are this exporter's habit; others write `''`.

**`#235`** is the bridge.
`CONTEXT_DEPENDENT_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION` has two attributes: a `representation_relation` and a `represented_product_relation`.
It ties the occurrence-shape `#238` to a relationship between two representations.

**`#236`** is a complex instance you can now read.
It is a `REPRESENTATION_RELATIONSHIP` between `#40` (the bracket's shape representation) and `#10` (the assembly's); it is *with a transformation*, `#237`; and it is specifically a *shape representation relationship*.
`REPRESENTATION_RELATIONSHIP_WITH_TRANSFORMATION` and `SHAPE_REPRESENTATION_RELATIONSHIP` are sibling subtypes of `REPRESENTATION_RELATIONSHIP`, and no single leaf names the pair.
So the instance is written externally, with their shared supertype listed as well, and the blocks in alphabetical order.

**`#237`** is the transformation, and it contains no numbers.
`ITEM_DEFINED_TRANSFORMATION` has two attributes beyond name and description: `transform_item_1` and `transform_item_2`, both representation items.
Here they are two axis placements: `#11`, the origin frame that sits in the bracket's own representation, and `#15`, a frame in the assembly's representation.
The transformation is *whatever rigid motion carries frame `#11` onto frame `#15`*.
Put the bracket's origin at `#15`'s origin, its Z along `#15`'s Z, its X along `#15`'s X.

**`#15`** is that target frame — at (0, 0, 0) with identity orientation, because the bracket sits at the assembly origin.
For pin-1 the corresponding record is `#19`, at (15, 10, 10); for pin-2 it is `#23`, at (45, 10, 10).
Those three points are the only coordinates in the assembly structure.

So the NAUO says *what* goes inside *what*, and its placement chain says *where*, and the two are joined through `#238` only — and only in the inverse direction, since `#238` points at the NAUO and nothing points at `#238` except `#235`, which nothing points at either.
From a NAUO, finding its position means asking "what `PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE` refers to me?" and then "what `CONTEXT_DEPENDENT_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION` refers to *that*?" — two more walks against the arrows before the references turn forward.

## The frame as a transform {#sec-assemblies-frame-transform}

```{.step source="clamp.step"}
#19 = AXIS2_PLACEMENT_3D('',#20,#21,#22);
#20 = CARTESIAN_POINT('',(15.,10.,10.));
#21 = DIRECTION('',(0.,0.,1.));
#22 = DIRECTION('',(1.,0.,-0.));
```

An `AXIS2_PLACEMENT_3D` has a `location`, an optional `axis` and an optional `ref_direction`.
The axis, normalised, is the frame's Z; the reference direction is projected perpendicular to Z and normalised to give X; Y is Z × X.
If the axis is omitted, Z is (0, 0, 1).
If the reference direction is omitted, Part 42's `first_proj_axis` projects (1, 0, 0), or (0, 1, 0) when Z is itself (±1, 0, 0): the fallback is specified, not an arbitrary perpendicular.
Three references, and the result is a complete right-handed coordinate frame — which is to say a rigid transformation: a rotation plus a translation, with no scaling and no reflection.

Placing pin-1, then, means: take the pin's geometry, whose coordinates are in its own frame (`#11` in the pin's representation — the pin stands on the origin with its axis along Z), and move it so that frame lands on `#19`.
Translation by (15, 10, 10), no rotation.
The pin's base circle, at z = 0 in its own file, is at z = 10 in the assembly: the top of the bracket.

::: {.callout-warning title="In the wild: Which frame is which"}
`ITEM_DEFINED_TRANSFORMATION` does not say which of its two items is the child's origin and which is the target.
In AP242 the schema already ties the items to the representations: `transform_item_1` must be used in `rep_1` and `transform_item_2` in `rep_2`.
What no schema says, and the CAx Implementor Forum's recommended practice does, is that `rep_1` is the child (component) and `rep_2` the parent (assembly).
This file follows both conventions: `#236` has `rep_1 = #40` (bracket) and `rep_2 = #10` (assembly); `#237` has item 1 in the bracket's representation and item 2 in the assembly's.
Not every exporter does.
A robust reader does not trust the order; it finds the frame that belongs to only one of the two representations — usually the target in the parent — and orients the transformation from that, because the child's origin frame is often shared by every representation in the file.
When both frames are the identity, as for the bracket here, getting it backwards is invisible — which is how the bug survives.
:::

## Walking the tree {#sec-assemblies-walking}

With the records understood, the procedure for reconstructing the assembly:

1. **Find the roots.** A root is a product definition that is nobody's `related_product_definition`. Here `#5`. A file may have several roots (a multi-body export, or several unrelated assemblies).
2. **Children of a definition** are the NAUOs whose `relating_product_definition` is it. For `#5`: `#239`, `#311`, `#317`.
3. **For each NAUO**, find the `PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE` that points at it, the `CONTEXT_DEPENDENT_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION` that points at *that*, and from there forward to the relationship, the transformation, and the two frames. If the chain is absent, try the mapped-item route below; if there is neither, readers place the child at identity, which is a convention of readers rather than a statement in the file.
4. **Geometry of a definition** is found through its own `PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE` and `SHAPE_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION`, as in @sec-product-to-shape.
5. **World position of a child** = parent's world transform composed with the local one. Recurse into the child's own NAUOs.

Convert translations and geometry to consistent length units before composing transforms between contexts.
Detect cycles along the active recursion path, but do not use a global visited set to suppress repeated definitions: that would drop legitimate occurrences and undercount a reused subassembly's children.

The **bill of materials** is steps 1, 2 and 5 without the geometry: walk the tree, group occurrences by `related_product_definition`, count.
For the clamp: bracket × 1, pin × 2.

Two sharings in this file are worth noticing because they are typical and because they catch tools that copy records around.
The origin frame `#11` is an item of *all three* shape representations — `#10`, `#40` and `#248` — and is `transform_item_1` in all three transformations.
One record, six roles.
And the three geometric contexts (`#27`, `#230`, `#302`) are textually identical but distinct records, one per product; each representation points at its own.

::: {.callout-warning title="In the wild: The category that says 'part'"}
This exporter writes `'part'` for all three products, including the assembly (`#32` points at `#7`, CLAMP-ASSY).
That is not a defect: these are AP214 files, and AP214's list of category names has no `'assembly'` in it.
AP203 and AP242 have no such list, and require `'assembly'` only on a product whose definition is declared an assembly definition; some exporters omit the category entirely.
Either way the category is no substitute for walking the `NEXT_ASSEMBLY_USAGE_OCCURRENCE` records.
The NAUOs are the truth: a definition with children is an assembly whatever its category says.
:::

## The other way: `MAPPED_ITEM` {#sec-assemblies-mapped-item}

Everything above is the *product-structure* way of placing components, and it is what the recommended practices call for.
There is a second, older mechanism that some exporters use for assemblies and some for repeated geometry *within* a part, and a reader must know both.

```{.step source="clamp.step"}
#400 = MAPPED_ITEM('',#401,#19);
#401 = REPRESENTATION_MAP(#11,#248);
```

A `MAPPED_ITEM` is a representation item — it sits in the *parent's* `SHAPE_REPRESENTATION.items`, next to the axis placements — that says "the representation `#248`, whose origin is `#11`, placed at frame `#19`."
The `REPRESENTATION_MAP` pairs a source representation with its origin; the mapped item pairs the map with a target.
Same information as `#235`–`#237`, two records instead of three, and no `PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE` on the NAUO.

When an exporter uses mapped items for an assembly, the NAUOs are still written — the product structure is unchanged — but the positions are in the parent's representation items rather than hanging off the NAUOs.
A reader that only knows the `CONTEXT_DEPENDENT_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION` route will find no placements and put every child at the origin.
If a NAUO has no placement chain, look in the parent's shape representation for `MAPPED_ITEM`s whose map's source is the child's representation.
That finds the placements; when several occurrences share one child representation, nothing in the file says which mapped item is which NAUO, and the pairing has to be left open.

Mapped items also appear where there is no assembly at all: a repeated sub-model, or a block of annotation geometry drawn once and placed a dozen times.
What they cannot do is instance a *feature*: a mapped item places a whole representation, and the faces of a bolt-hole pattern belong to the solid's one closed shell.
There the mapped item is simply an instancing mechanism, and the "child" representation is not a product's shape but an anonymous representation containing the repeated geometry.

## Deeper trees and other variations {#sec-assemblies-deeper-trees}

The clamp is two levels.
A real assembly is many, and nothing changes: each intermediate node is a product definition with NAUOs pointing at it (as a child) and NAUOs pointing from it (as a parent), and its shape representation holds frames for its own children.
World transforms compose down the tree.

Variations you will meet:

- **Several shape representations per part** — a B-rep and a tessellation, say. The `REPRESENTATION_RELATIONSHIP` in the placement chain names *which* representation of the child is being placed, and a part may need a placement per representation.
- **A NAUO with no placement chain at all.** Legal: product structure may be exchanged without positions. Readers put the child at identity, which is right for files from systems that flatten everything to the world frame first and a guess otherwise.
- **`ASSEMBLY_COMPONENT_USAGE` with quantity.** All three protocols allow a `QUANTIFIED_ASSEMBLY_COMPONENT_USAGE` — one relationship carrying a count instead of one NAUO per occurrence — for parts like fasteners where individual positions are not modelled. Rare in CAD exports.
- **Promissory and specified-higher usages.** `SPECIFIED_HIGHER_USAGE_OCCURRENCE` names an occurrence deeper in the tree from a level above, carrying both the upper usage and the next usage it derives from; `PROMISSORY_USAGE_OCCURRENCE` adds nothing to a NAUO and marks a usage that is intended rather than realised. They exist for configuration management and almost never appear in geometry exchange.

::: {.callout-important title="In brief"}
The assembly tree is a set of `NEXT_ASSEMBLY_USAGE_OCCURRENCE` edges from parent definition to child definition; one edge is one occurrence, and a bill of materials is a count of edges per child.
Position is separate: a `PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE` on the NAUO, a `CONTEXT_DEPENDENT_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION`, a three-way relationship record, an `ITEM_DEFINED_TRANSFORMATION` naming two frames, and the target frame in the parent's representation.
The frame is the transform.
`MAPPED_ITEM` is the alternative route, and a reader must handle both.
:::
